fields.oneLiner: GalatSawaal takes the questions a NEET repeater got wrong in Sunday's mock test and sends them back as a 15-minute set on Wednesday, Saturday and the Thursday after.
fields.jobStory:
When I finish a Sunday mock at my coaching institute and the question-wise report comes out on Tuesday, I want the forty-odd questions I got wrong to come back to me on their own over the next two weeks, so I can stop losing the same rotational-motion numerical in three tests in a row.

Who has this job: NEET repeaters, droppers, in the Sikar and Kota test-series batches. Eighteen to twenty years old, second attempt, sitting a full mock every Sunday and getting a rank list with a question-wise breakdown. You find them in the dropper batch WhatsApp groups, in the forty-odd paid libraries around Nehru Park in Sikar, and on r/NEETpreparation where somebody posts about their error notebook roughly every week.

What they do instead: a physical error notebook. Every teacher recommends it, everybody starts one in April. Of the 23 droppers in my cousin's batch that I spoke to, 19 had a notebook and 4 had opened it in the last month. Copying one question by hand takes four to six minutes, so a forty-mistake test is three hours of copying before any revision starts. The ones who quit the notebook just re-read the solution PDF once on Tuesday and never see that question again.
fields.trafficTestNotes:
Two sources, 28 August to 9 September 2026.

1. Telegram. I asked three admins of NEET dropper channels for permission and posted in all three: one channel with 41k members, two with about 8k each. Posts went out 28 Aug, 1 Sep and 5 Sep. Telegram shows view counts per post: 12,300, 3,050 and 2,700. Framer analytics shows 388 clicks from Telegram, and 44 of those signed up. I paid 500 rupees to the 41k admin to pin the post for 24 hours. The other two were free.

2. Reddit, r/NEETpreparation. One text post on 2 Sep, about 400 words on the error-notebook problem with the link at the bottom rather than the top. 214 upvotes, 61 comments, and Reddit's own insights say 31,400 views. 129 clicks, 19 signups, zero spend.

So: 517 visits, 63 signups, 12.2%, total spend 500 rupees. Reddit converted better (14.7%) than Telegram (11.3%), which surprised me. I think that is because the Reddit post actually described the problem and the Telegram one was two lines and a link. Twelve percent is high for cold traffic, but the page only asks for an email and promises the first version free, so it is a cheap yes and I would not read it as demand for a paid product yet.
